opus-5.5.text:
I think healthcare is one of the best places to do grounded alignment work, for a few reasons.

First, the stakes are real and immediate. When a model gives medical advice, the consequences of being subtly wrong, overconfident, or sycophantic aren't hypothetical. They show up in people's lives. That forces you to take questions like "is this model actually helpful, or just persuasive?" seriously in a way that a lot of benchmark settings don't.

Second, healthcare already looks like the problems we expect to face with more capable systems. A lot of alignment comes down to scalable oversight: how do you supervise a system whose outputs you can't easily verify yourself? Medicine is full of that. Many patients can't evaluate an answer, and even physicians often disagree or would need significant time to check a complex response. So you're naturally studying how to get reliable signal from imperfect, expensive, sometimes conflicting human judgments. That's what we'll need when models outperform their evaluators in more domains.

Third, there's a lot of rich, structured human expertise to draw on. You have clinicians who can articulate why an answer is good or bad. Is it safe, does it reflect consensus, does it communicate uncertainty well, does it fit the person's actual situation? That lets you build rubrics and evaluation frameworks that are much more nuanced than "thumbs up, thumbs down," and you can study where expert and lay preferences diverge.

Fourth, it pushes on hard behavioral questions. When should a model defer, refuse, or escalate to a human? How should it handle ambiguity, or a user who wants reassurance more than accuracy? Those are calibration, honesty, and appropriate-deference problems, and they generalize well beyond medicine.

Finally, it's a domain where getting it right has enormous upside. Billions of people lack good access to medical expertise. So the work isn't only about making models less harmful. It's about making them trustworthy enough to deliver real benefit. I find that combination of high stakes, hard oversight problems, and real-world impact makes healthcare a great testbed. Lessons learned there tend to transfer to the broader project of building AI systems we can actually rely on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that healthcare is one of the few domains where the hard problems of alignment show up concretely, with real stakes, and with a lot of existing infrastructure for thinking about them.

Take the question of what it even means for a model to be helpful and honest. In a lot of settings that's fuzzy. In medicine it's not. If a model gives a confident answer about a drug interaction and it's wrong, someone can get hurt. So you're forced to actually operationalize things like calibration, knowing when to defer, communicating uncertainty to someone who isn't an expert, and handling the case where the user is asking for something that might not be in their interest. Those are core alignment problems, and healthcare gives you a setting where you can measure whether you're making progress rather than arguing about it in the abstract.

The second thing is that medicine already has a culture around this. There's a long tradition of thinking about how a practitioner should behave when they're uncertain, how to weigh patient autonomy against harm, how to disclose risk, how to escalate. Clinicians have norms, there are review processes, there's a notion of standard of care. You don't have to invent evaluation frameworks from scratch. You can borrow from how we assess human doctors, which is itself imperfect, but it gives you a starting point that's much richer than a generic benchmark.

Third, the domain exposes a lot of the gap between "sounds right" and "is right." Models are very good at producing fluent, plausible medical text. Early on we found that answers could read as expert and still contain errors that a physician would catch immediately. That's exactly the failure mode we worry about more broadly, where capabilities outpace our ability to verify. Working on that in healthcare, with expert raters, adversarial questions, and real clinical workflows, taught us things that generalize about how to evaluate models we can't fully trust.

And finally, it's a place where getting it right actually matters for a lot of people. Access to good medical information is deeply unequal. If you can build systems that are genuinely safe and reliable in this setting, the upside is enormous. That makes it easier to attract people who care about both the technical problems and the impact, and it keeps the work honest, because you can't hand-wave the safety side when deployment is on the table.

astra-6.text:
I think healthcare makes a lot of the questions we care about in AI safety and alignment very concrete. You’re not just asking whether a model can produce a correct answer. You’re asking whether it knows when it doesn’t have enough information, whether it should ask a clarifying question, and when it should defer to a clinician. Those are alignment problems, and getting them right really matters.

It also forces you to think carefully about what success means. A response can sound helpful and still be unsafe. And there may not be one objectively right answer: the right decision can depend on a patient’s preferences, their circumstances, and the tradeoffs they’re willing to make. So you need systems that can support that decision-making without simply substituting their own judgment.

What makes healthcare particularly valuable is that there’s a substantial body of expertise and practice we can draw on to evaluate these behaviors. That doesn’t make evaluation easy, but it gives us a concrete setting for developing and testing safety techniques, with a direct benefit to people if we succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think healthcare is valuable because it makes a lot of the abstract questions in AI safety very concrete. What does it mean for a model to be helpful? How should it communicate uncertainty? When should it answer, ask a clarifying question, or defer to a human? Those questions matter a lot when someone might act on the response.

It also pushes us beyond the idea that alignment is just following instructions. A patient might ask for reassurance when the appropriate response is to encourage them to seek care. A clinician might want a quick answer, but the model needs to make an important uncertainty visible. So you have to think carefully about whose interests you're serving and what a good outcome actually looks like.

And there's a tremendous upside. If we can make these systems reliable and useful, they could help many more people access high-quality care. That combination—meaningful benefits and real consequences for getting things wrong—makes healthcare a compelling place to develop and test safety techniques.
